items.stem: Why does the Global VM Lock (GVL) in CRuby limit speedup for CPU-bound threads?

options.text: Only one thread runs Ruby bytecode at a time, so CPU work is not truly parallel
options.rationale: The GVL serialises Ruby execution; threads help mainly with IO waits.

options.text: Threads are disabled entirely in CRuby
options.rationale: Threads exist; the GVL just serialises bytecode execution.

options.text: The GVL speeds up all CPU work automatically
options.rationale: It constrains, not accelerates, CPU-bound parallelism.
Fibers are cooperative and still under the same model.

items.explanation: The GVL serialises Ruby execution; threads help mainly with IO waits.

items.stem: Select TWO accurate statements about method lookup in Ruby's object model.

options.text: Modules prepended to a class are searched before the class's own methods
options.rationale: prepend inserts the module earlier in the ancestor chain.

options.text: The ancestors array reflects the order methods are searched
options.rationale: Lookup follows the ancestors order from the receiver upward.

options.text: Singleton methods are never consulted during lookup
options.rationale: The singleton class is searched first.

options.text: include inserts a module before the class itself in the chain
options.rationale: include inserts after the class; prepend inserts before.

items.explanation: prepend inserts the module earlier in the ancestor chain.

items.stem: What is the risk of memoising with @value ||= compute when compute may return nil or false?

options.text: Every access re-runs compute because the falsey result is never cached
options.rationale: ||= treats nil/false as unset, defeating memoisation for those values.
The issue is re-computation, not type.
No error is raised; it just recomputes.

items.explanation: ||= treats nil/false as unset, defeating memoisation for those values.
